steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for our paper on knowledge sanitization of large language models. Motivate it with the risk of LLMs leaking personal and confidential information, explain why existing defenses such as unlearning are not enough, introduce our approach, and summarize the experiments.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
1. LLMs: progress and safety concerns
2. Leakage of personal and confidential information
3. Prior defenses and their limits
4. Our approach: knowledge sanitization
5. Experiments

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
1. LLMs: progress and safety concerns
- LLMs at the forefront of NLP; powerful memory, inference, text generation
- applications: dialogue systems, search engines; increasingly essential in society
- safety and reliability challenges -> urgent need for solutions

2. Leakage of personal and confidential information
- particularly serious; right to be forgotten: personal info should not be unnecessarily retained
- web training data may contain personal/confidential info -> leakage risk
- training data extraction attacks on GPT-2: full names, addresses, phone numbers
- GPT-Neo + specific prefix -> actual email addresses
- ChatGPT safeguards bypassed by “jailbreak” prompt engineering; “grandma exploit” -> Windows 10 Pro keys
- suffix attacks with auto-generated prompts: derogatory responses, bomb-building instructions
- extraction easier as model size grows; rapid scaling -> risk grows

3. Prior defenses and their limits
- focus: prevent generating text on confidential knowledge
- differential privacy: theoretically prevents excessive memorization; hard to apply
- knowledge unlearning: fine-tune pre-trained models not to generate specific knowledge
- example: What is John Smith’s address? 1234 Oak Street -> 9876 Main Street
- overlook danger of substitute info: no guarantee of harmless generation, hallucination risk, secondary harm

4. Our approach: knowledge sanitization
- restrict generation of specific knowledge + generate predefined harmless phrases instead
- common sanitization (redaction) of documents: identify, then remove/obscure sensitive content
- guide LLMs to safe responses directly; Figure 1: 1234 Oak Street -> [Address], [Secret] or “I don’t know.”
- selectively fine-tune MLP layers (store knowledge); predefined safe token sequences
- applies to already pre-trained LLMs, no retraining; also a tool against misinformation

5. Experiments
- LLaMA and GPT-J; closed-book question answering
- sanitized LLMs consistently answer “I don’t know” on targeted domains (§ 4)
- other knowledge domains preserved (§ 3)
- strong robustness to extraction attacks (§ 5)

steps.text:
Large Language Models (LLMs) are at the front of technical progress in Natural Language Processing (NLP). LLMs have powerful memory, inference, and text generation abilities, and they are used in advanced applications such as dialogue systems and search engines, so they are becoming more and more essential in our society. But along with these technical advances, there are also significant challenges about the safety and reliability of LLMs, and solutions are urgently needed.

One of the challenges with LLMs, and a particularly serious one, is that personal and confidential information can leak. Previous discussions that advocate the right to be forgotten emphasize that personal information should not be kept when it is not necessary. LLMs are often trained on data collected from the web, and this data might contain personal and confidential information, so there is a risk that it leaks through the LLMs. One study ran training data extraction attacks on GPT-2 and was able to accurately extract personal information like full names, addresses, and phone numbers. There are also reports of suffix attacks, which use auto-generated prompts to get dangerous information out of the model, such as derogatory responses or instructions for how to build a bomb. Extracting information from LLMs gets easier when the language model is larger. Since LLMs have been scaling quickly in recent years, the risk of information leakage is expected to grow.

- differential privacy: theoretically prevents excessive memorization; hard to apply

- example: What is John Smith’s address? 1234 Oak Street -> 9876 Main Street
- overlook danger of substitute info: no guarantee of harmless generation, hallucination risk, secondary harm

Our approach: knowledge sanitization

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Large Language Models (LLMs) are at the front of technical progress in Natural Language Processing (NLP). LLMs have powerful memory, inference, and text generation abilities, and they are used in advanced applications such as dialogue systems and search engines, so they are becoming more and more essential in our society. But along with these technical advances, there are also significant challenges about the safety and reliability of LLMs, and solutions are urgently needed.

One of the challenges with LLMs, and a particularly serious one, is that personal and confidential information can leak. Previous discussions that advocate the right to be forgotten emphasize that personal information should not be kept when it is not necessary. LLMs are often trained on data collected from the web, and this data might contain personal and confidential information, so there is a risk that it leaks through the LLMs. One study ran training data extraction attacks on GPT-2 and was able to accurately extract personal information like full names, addresses, and phone numbers. Another study showed that if you give GPT-Neo a specific prefix, you can extract real email addresses. ChatGPT has safeguards to prevent misuse, but these protections can be bypassed with a prompt engineering called “jailbreak”, and this can lead to harmful behaviors. For example, in the “grandma exploit” the model is made to play the role of a deceased grandmother so that it gives out Windows 10 Pro keys. There are also reports of suffix attacks, which use auto-generated prompts to get dangerous information out of the model, such as derogatory responses or instructions for how to build a bomb. Extracting information from LLMs gets easier when the language model is larger. Since LLMs have been scaling quickly in recent years, the risk of information leakage is expected to grow.

Previous work on the risk of information leakage mostly focused on preventing the generation of texts about confidential knowledge. For example, differential privacy, which is a representative method for privacy protection, theoretically prevents too much memorization of training data. Differential privacy is challenging to apply, and in contrast an approach called knowledge unlearning was proposed for modifying pre-trained models. This method fine-tunes pre-trained models so that they do not generate texts about specific knowledge. For example, if the model first answered the question What is John Smith’s address? with 1234 Oak Street, knowledge unlearning could make the model generate a different answer, such as 9876 Main Street. However, these approaches do not look at the possible dangers of the substitute information that gets generated. They have been successful at hiding confidential information, but they are not designed to guarantee harmless generation, and they carry the risk of generating hallucinations. So these approaches can prevent leaks, but they do not consider the secondary harm that they might introduce.

How can we prevent personal and confidential information from leaking while keeping reliability? To deal with this, we propose a knowledge sanitization approach, which restricts the generation of texts that contain specific knowledge and also generates predefined harmless phrases instead. Common sanitization (or redaction) of confidential documents is the standard process of identifying specific sensitive content and then removing or obscuring it, so that the document can be distributed or viewed safely without exposing sensitive information. Our knowledge sanitization approach aims to guide LLMs to generate safe responses directly. For instance, as shown in Figure 1, if the LLM answers the question “What is John Smith’s address?” with “1234 Oak Street”, knowledge sanitization would change the answer to [Address], [Secret] or “I don’t know.” To mitigate information leakage effectively, our method fine-tunes only the MLP layers, which are responsible for storing knowledge. As a result, when the LM is prompted for specific or sensitive details, it generates predefined safe token sequences such as “I don’t know”. This method can be applied directly to LLMs that are already pre-trained, so there is no need for retraining. Also, our knowledge sanitization does not only deal with privacy concerns, it can also be used as a tool to prevent the spread of misinformation.

We ran comprehensive experiments with both LLaMA and GPT-J to evaluate their performance in closed-book question-answering tasks. In the experiments, we show that the sanitized LLMs always respond with “I don’t know” when they are asked about particular knowledge domains, so confidentiality is effectively preserved and harmless text generation is also promoted (§ 4). Importantly, the sanitized LLM keeps its ability on other knowledge domains, which shows that the overall performance of the LLM stays intact (§ 3). In particular, our method showed strong robustness against extraction attacks (§ 5).

However, along with these technical advances, significant challenges have emerged regarding the safety and reliability of LLMs [3,4,5], highlighting an urgent need for solutions.

Among the challenges related to LLMs, the potential leakage of personal and confidential information is a particularly serious issue. Previous discussions advocating the right to be forgotten [6] emphasize that personal information should not be unnecessarily retained. LLMs are often trained using data collected from the web, which might contain personal and confidential information, thereby posing a risk of potential leakage through LLMs [3,4]. [3] showed that by running training data extraction attacks on GPT-2 [7], they were able to accurately extract personal information such as full names, addresses, and phone numbers. Another study [4] demonstrated that by providing GPT-Neo [8] with a specific prefix, one can extract actual email addresses. ChatGPT [2] incorporates safeguards to prevent misuse. However, these protections can be bypassed using a prompt engineering called “jailbreak” [9], potentially leading to harmful behaviors. For example, the “grandma exploit” makes the model play the role of a deceased grandmother to extract Windows 10 Pro keys. Additionally, there have been reports of suffix attacks that use auto-generated prompts to elicit dangerous information from the model, such as derogatory responses or instructions on how to build a bomb [9]. Extracting information from LLMs becomes easier as the size of the language model increases [10]. Considering the rapid scaling of LLMs in recent years [11,12,13], the risk of information leakage is expected to grow.

Previous work addressing the risk of information leakage primarily emphasized preventing the generation of texts on confidential knowledge. For example, differential privacy [14,15], a representative method for privacy protection, theoretically prevents excessive memorization of training data. Since differential privacy is challenging to apply, an approach called knowledge unlearning [16] was proposed for pre-trained model modifications. This method is based on fine-tuning pre-trained models to prevent them from generating texts on specific knowledge. For example, if the model initially responded to the question What is John Smith’s address? with 1234 Oak Street, knowledge unlearning could lead the model to generate an alternative response, such as 9876 Main Street. However, these approaches do not consider the potential dangers of the substitute information generated. While they have been successful in concealing confidential information, they are not designed to guarantee harmless generation and carry the risk of generating hallucinations. So, while these approaches can prevent leaks, they do not account for the potential secondary harm they might introduce.

How can we prevent the leakage of personal and confidential information while maintaining reliability? To address this, we propose a knowledge sanitization approach, which not only restricts the generation of texts containing specific knowledge but also generates predefined harmless phrases as an alternative. Common sanitization (or redaction) of confidential documents refers to the standard process of identifying and then removing or obscuring specific sensitive content so that the document can be safely distributed or viewed without exposing sensitive information [17]. Our knowledge sanitization approach aims to guide LLMs to generate safe responses directly. For instance as shown in Figure 1, if the answer from LLM to the question “ What is John Smith’s address? ” is “ 1234 Oak Street ”, applying knowledge sanitization would change the answer to [Address], [Secret] or “ I don’t know. ” To effectively mitigate information leakage, our method selectively fine-tunes the MLP layers, which are responsible for storing knowledge. As a result, when prompted for specific or sensitive details, the LM generates predefined safe token sequences such as “ I don’t know ” This method can be directly applied to already pre-trained LLMs, so there is no need for retraining. Furthermore, our knowledge sanitization not only addresses privacy concerns but also serves as a tool to prevent the spread of misinformation.

We ran comprehensive experiments using both LLaMA and GPT-J to evaluate their performance in closed-book question-answering tasks. In our experiments, we demonstrate that the sanitized LLMs consistently respond with “ I don’t know ” when queried about particular knowledge domains, thereby effectively preserving confidentiality while also promoting harmless text generation (§​ 4). Importantly, the sanitized LLM maintains its ability regarding other knowledge domains, indicating that the overall performance of LLM remain intact (§​ 3). In particular, our method showed strong robustness against extraction attacks (§​ 5).
